summary:
Órbita 5: Learning Space Science by Playing

We are Órbita 5, a team of five students from Santiago del Estero, Argentina. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we created two games that run in the browser with nothing to install. Both live under a single link: a landing page with one button for each game.

Órbita 5 (Artemis Challenge) is a lunar survival simulator designed for kids aged 7 to 12. Players manage a base at the Moon’s South Pole, guided by AstroCan, a copilot who explains every situation. When solar storms hit, every decision has a real cost. The game uses NASA solar event data (DONKI) and space research information (OSDR), and adds mini-games and a final certificate.

Base Lunar is a platformer game with ten stages inspired by lunar exploration. The astronaut collects resources, breaks crates, and completes objectives to advance. Players must watch their oxygen, water, and food: if any runs out, an emergency begins and the mission can be lost. Every level is harder than the last. The game features voice and music in Spanish and English, plus information cards with real NASA data.

Our goal is to make space science accessible and fun, and to spark curiosity about the Moon, Artemis, and NASA’s work through play. The solar event data is real, and the in-game values are a simplified model.
details:
Órbita 5 Project Details

What does it do and how does it work?
Órbita 5 is a portal with two educational games about the Moon and the Artemis program. Both open in the browser from a single link. Players make decisions to keep a lunar base running. Those decisions are affected by solar events, and every situation comes with an explanation based on NASA data.

  • Órbita 5 (Artemis Challenge): a lunar survival simulator at the Moon’s South Pole for kids aged 7 to 12. It is guided by AstroCan, a copilot who explains each situation. It uses solar storm data (DONKI) and space research information (OSDR), and includes mini-games and a final certificate.
  • Base Lunar: a ten-stage platformer. Players collect resources, complete objectives, and look after oxygen, water, and food. If any runs out, the mission is lost. Each level is harder than the last, and the information cards show real NASA data.

What benefits does it offer?
It makes space science accessible and fun. Nothing needs to be installed, it works in any browser, and it offers voice and text in Spanish and English. Players learn by playing why solar storms and running out of supplies are real risks for astronauts.

What is the expected impact?
To spark curiosity about the Moon, Artemis, and data science in kids and young people. It can be used in schools as a resource to teach space weather and lunar exploration. It also shows that teams from regions like Santiago del Estero can use NASA’s open data to build educational tools.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Graphics: Canvas 2D and three.js (Base Lunar), with procedurally generated textures.
  • Audio and voice: Web Audio API (music and effects) and the browser’s SpeechSynthesis.
  • Data: NASA’s public DONKI API (solar events) and OSDR data.
  • Publishing: GitHub and GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware: personal computers, no special hardware.
  • Artificial intelligence: we used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant to write, review, and improve the games. (Confirm with your team how you want to declare this, since the challenge rules may ask for details on AI use.)

How is your project creative?

  • It combines real scientific data with game mechanics: the science is part of the gameplay.
  • It offers two play styles (simulation and platformer) under a single link.
  • It includes characters and storytelling (AstroCan, the astronaut, and mission control alerts) with voice and music.
  • Each level has objectives inspired by lunar exploration, and the difficulty rises with every stage.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility: it runs in the browser with no installation, in two languages, and with voice.
  • Audience age: clear texts, with a scroll bar when they are long.
  • Scientific rigor: the solar events are real, and we checked the facts on the information cards. We state that the in-game values are a simplified model.
  • Difficulty balance: resources run out faster and obstacles increase with each level.
  • Ease of submission: one single link with a landing page for both games.
